records.text: The nested arrangement of organisms into groups within groups (species within genera, genera within families, and so on) results from the modified descendants of a single progenitor diverging in character while less divergent forms are exterminated.
records.label: Descent with divergence and extinction produces groups subordinate to groups

records.text: The 'something more' than mere resemblance that naturalists seek in the Natural System is closeness of descent, which is the only known cause of similarity among organisms and is partially revealed by classifications.

records.label: Characters least modified by adaptation are most constant and useful in classification

records.text: The relative value of groups such as orders, sub-orders, families, sub-families and genera is, at least at present, almost arbitrary, as shown by groups being raised in rank merely because more allied species were discovered.
records.label: Higher taxonomic ranks are almost arbitrary

records.text: A natural arrangement of groups must be strictly genealogical, but branches that are equally closely related to a common progenitor may differ greatly in how much they have been modified, and these differing amounts of difference are what is expressed by ranking them as different genera, families or orders.
records.label: Branches equally related by descent can differ greatly in amount of modification

records.text: Domestic and natural varieties fall into groups subordinate to groups (sub-varieties under varieties under species) for the same reason species do, namely closeness of descent combined with various degrees of modification.

records.text: However trifling a character, if it occurs throughout many species with very different habits of life it can be explained only by inheritance from a common parent, and so has high value for classification; for the same reason rudimentary structures can be as useful as other parts.
records.label: Characters shared across species with very different habits indicate common inheritance

records.text: Animals from very distinct lines of descent can become adapted to similar conditions and so acquire a close external resemblance; such analogical or adaptive resemblances conceal rather than reveal blood-relationship, so they are almost worthless for classification between groups, although the same characters can indicate true affinity within a group.
records.label: Distinct lineages adapted to similar conditions converge in external form

records.text: Larger and more dominant groups tend to keep increasing in size and to supplant smaller, feebler groups, which is why all organisms, recent and extinct, fall into a few great orders, still fewer classes, and a single natural system.
records.label: Expanding dominant groups explain why all life falls into a few great classes

records.text: Aberrant or osculant groups are the surviving remnants of failing groups that suffered heavy extinction; consequently they are generally represented by very few species, and those species are usually very distinct from each other.
records.label: Aberrant groups are species-poor relicts of extinction

records.text: When a member of one group shows a real affinity to a quite distinct group, the affinity is usually general rather than to any particular species, because it retains characters of an ancient common progenitor of both groups.
records.label: Affinities of one group to another are usually general, not to any single species

records.label: Homologous parts change shape and size but keep the same relative connexions

records.text: The shared pattern of homologous organs within a class is explained by descent from an ancient progenitor (an archetype) that already had that pattern, which natural selection then modified by slight successive steps for different uses without transposing parts.
records.label: Unity of type reflects a common progenitor's pattern modified by slight steps

records.text: Serial homologies within one individual (skull and vertebrae, jaws and legs of crustaceans, floral parts and leaves) arise because the progenitors of vertebrates, articulates and flowering plants had many repeated similar parts, which natural selection adapted to diverse purposes while inheritance retained a fundamental resemblance.

records.text: Whenever an embryo or larva becomes active and must provide for itself, it is as perfectly adapted to its conditions of life as the adult, and such adaptations can make the larvae of allied species differ as much as or more than their adults, though most larvae still follow the law of embryonic resemblance.

records.text: Rudimentary organs vary greatly in development among individuals of the same species, and the degree of reduction of the same organ can differ much between closely allied species; because they are useless, their variations are not checked by natural selection.

records.text: By analogy, probably all organisms that have ever lived on earth have descended from a single primordial form.

records.text: The only distinction between species and well-marked varieties is that varieties are known or believed to be connected by intermediate gradations at present, whereas species were connected by them in the past; species should therefore be treated, like genera, as combinations made for convenience.
records.label: Species differ from varieties only in their intermediates having existed formerly

records.text: The most important cause of organic change is the mutual relation of organism to organism, in which the improvement of one form causes the improvement or extermination of others; this is almost independent of changes, even sudden ones, in physical conditions.

records.text: The whole history of the world as known from geology is only a small fragment of the time that has elapsed since the first organism, the progenitor of all later forms, came into existence.
records.label: Known geological history is a fragment of the time since the first organism

records.text: Each mental power and capacity must have been acquired gradually, so psychology will rest on this foundation, and light will be thrown on the origin of man and his history.
records.label: Every mental power was acquired by gradation

records.text: Very few living species will leave descendants in the far future, and those that will prevail and give rise to new dominant species will be the common, widespread species of the larger, dominant groups.

records.text: Since all living forms are lineal descendants of forms that lived long before the Silurian epoch, the ordinary succession by generation has never once been broken and no cataclysm has ever desolated the whole world.
records.label: Succession by generation has never been broken by a world-wide cataclysm

records.text: Because natural selection works solely by and for the good of each being, all bodily and mental endowments will tend to progress towards perfection.
records.label: Natural selection makes endowments tend towards perfection

records.text: The varied and interdependent forms of life were produced by laws still acting: growth with reproduction; inheritance; variability caused by external conditions and by use and disuse; a rate of increase high enough to cause a struggle for life and so natural selection, which in turn causes divergence of character and extinction of less improved forms.
records.label: The 'entangled bank' laws produce the diversity of living forms

records.text: As long as fortuitous variation and the survival of the fittest are accepted as sufficient explanations in biology, they will tend to hold back careful investigation of the real physical causes of organic form.
records.label: Reliance on chance variation and natural selection stalls inquiry into physical causes

records.text: The material parts of living things (cells, tissues, shells, bones, leaves, flowers) are portions of matter whose particles have been moved, moulded and shaped in obedience to the laws of physics.
records.label: Cells, tissues, shells, bones, leaves and flowers are shaped by the laws of physics

records.text: The problems of the form of living things are, in the first instance, mathematical problems and their problems of growth are essentially physical problems, so morphology is a branch of physical science.
records.label: Problems of organic form are mathematical and problems of growth are physical

records.text: However complex living processes are, no physical law (including those of chemistry, surface action and osmosis) is known to be broken by the working of the body.
records.label: No known physical law is transgressed by the bodily mechanism

records.text: The form of any portion of matter, living or dead, can be read as a diagram of forces: from the shape of a solid one can deduce the forces that produced and maintain it, and from the shape of a fluid the forces currently acting on it, so an organism's conformation is explained by a balance of forces.
records.label: The form of an object is a diagram of the forces acting or that have acted on it

records.text: Like other fluid bodies, the surface of a cell such as an Amoeba carries a surface tension that depends on the substance it touches, and this surface tension strongly affects the cell's form.
records.label: Surface tension at a cell's boundary strongly affects its form

records.text: The protoplasm of an Amoeba deforms and flows under the slightest pressure, so it is a fluid, but it is far more viscous than water, like treacle, and this viscosity slows its changes of shape.
records.label: Protoplasm behaves as a highly viscous fluid that changes shape under force

records.text: There is no clear rule for deciding what is 'vital', and the properties of organisms cannot be clearly split into those of physical origin and those peculiar to living things, so physical analysis must proceed piece by piece.
records.label: Vital phenomena cannot be cleanly divided into physical and non-physical ones

records.text: In development, variation and inheritance, material elements such as the spermatozoon, nucleus, chromosomes or germ-plasm never act as matter alone, but only as seats of energy and centres of force.
records.label: Nuclei, chromosomes and germ-plasm act only as seats of energy and centres of force

records.text: Since muscular work available scales as the cube of linear size while the rate of energy supply, depending on respiratory surface, scales only as the square, a larger fish should achieve a much higher burst speed than a smaller one but travel a similar distance over a year, and smaller individuals should fatigue faster and have less staying power.

records.label: Doubling gravity would make terrestrial animals short-legged or serpent-like

records.text: Throughout morphology, surface tends to keep pace with volume through changes of form, such as intestinal villi and folds, the shark's spiral valve, and brain convolutions whose complexity is correlated with animal size, so that a roughly constant ratio of surface to mass is maintained.
records.label: Folded surfaces such as villi and brain convolutions keep surface in step with mass

records.text: The form of all small organisms is largely independent of gravity and mainly due to surface tension, acting either now or at an earlier stage before the form was made rigid, so small organisms tend strongly toward spherical and other simple surface-tension forms that do not occur in the external form of large animals.

records.text: The optimum temperature for growth is much the same, about 26 °C, for the common plants of temperate climates, and considerably higher for plants of warmer regions such as melon and maize.

records.text: Van’t Hoff’s law, that reaction velocity is multiplied by a constant factor for each degree of temperature rise, applies with qualifications to growth, so that growth has a temperature coefficient (about 2 to 3 per 10 °C, of the same order as chemical reactions).
records.label: Growth has a van’t Hoff temperature coefficient like a chemical reaction

records.text: Growth rate has an optimum temperature because temperature both accelerates growth according to van’t Hoff’s law and progressively damages or fatigues the organism, so the optimum curve is a complex resultant rather than a primary phenomenon.

records.text: In fishes such as plaice and haddock, and in man, growth is slower in winter than in summer, as if an annual sine curve were superimposed on the growth curve, and the amplitude of this fluctuation dies away as growth slows, giving a damped sine curve.
records.label: Seasonal growth in fish and man follows a damped sine curve

records.text: Century-smoothed annual ring widths of Arizona yellow pines show that the climate of Arizona over the past 500 years fluctuated with a regular period of almost exactly 150 years, probably mainly in moisture rather than temperature.

records.text: A large part of growth, in animals and more conspicuously in plants, depends on turgor and osmotic conditions: the velocity of growth depends largely on the amount of water taken into the cells as well as on chemical metabolism.

records.text: In brine-shrimps (Artemia), increasing salinity changes the relative rates of growth of body parts, the abdomen growing relatively longer compared with the cephalothorax the salter the water, so that forms described as distinct species correspond to ranges of water density.
records.label: Brine-shrimp abdomen grows relatively longer the saltier the water

records.text: The normal curve of growth of an organism closely resembles the velocity curve of an autocatalytic chemical reaction, with a phase of increasing acceleration, a phase in which limiting conditions reduce acceleration, and usually a final phase of retardation and loss of mass; but only a resemblance, not an identity, can yet be asserted.
records.label: The organic curve of growth resembles the velocity curve of chemical autocatalysis

records.text: Substances inside and outside the organism, such as thyroid and pituitary secretions or iodine compounds, can accelerate growth in a way that changes not only the size but the form or proportions of the organism.
records.label: Internal secretions and other substances accelerate growth and alter proportions

records.text: Since forms, including exaggerated ones such as the great Secondary reptiles and Tertiary mammals, can arise from changes in growth, natural selection is needed to explain their disappearance rather than their appearance; in general its function is not to originate but to remove.
records.label: Natural selection removes forms rather than originating them

records.text: After its early maximum, the velocity of regenerative growth (tadpole tails) falls off inversely as some power of the time since injury, approximately as 1/T^2, so that V T^2 is nearly constant.

records.text: The nucleus is almost always spherical because its fluid substance does not mix with the surrounding protoplasm, so it is bounded by a film of uniform surface tension and immersed in a medium transmitting uniform fluid pressure; where the cytoplasm becomes more solid (as in muscle cells or mucus-laden epithelial cells) the pressure becomes unsymmetrical and the nucleus is deformed.

records.text: The alveolar 'reticulum' seen in the nucleus and cytoplasm is a froth or foam produced by the interacting surface tensions of two intermixed fluids of similar density striving to separate, and is not inherent in the nature of protoplasm.

records.text: Fixation preserves the general outward form of small organisms and cells, but the minute internal networks and granules described as the structure of protoplasm are to a large extent artefacts of coagulating fixatives, although larger structures such as nucleus, vacuoles, centrosomes and the spindle are really present in the living cell.

records.text: In the bipolar field between the centrosomes the nucleus as a whole behaves as a body more permeable than the cytoplasm and is drawn in between the poles, whereas its chromatin, once broken up, behaves like a diamagnetic body, is repelled to the weaker parts of the field, and so collects in a peripheral circle on the equatorial plane.
records.label: Chromatin behaves as a diamagnetic body and moves to the equatorial plane

records.text: Differences of electric potential between cell constituents, and between parts of the egg, play a great part in cell division; the potential difference between animal and vegetative poles of a fertilised egg fluctuates or reverses at successive segmentations, and the electrical difference of chromatin is greatest at mitosis.
records.label: Differences of electric potential play a great part in cell division

records.text: In all cells the mechanical process of division must be explained as the result of a conflict between surface tension and its opposing forces, the division plane being set in the equatorial plane of the polar field.
records.label: Every cell division results from conflict between surface tension and opposing forces

records.text: Because later spermatozoa fail to enter the egg after the first, an immediate consequence of sperm entry is an increase in the surface tension of the egg.

records.text: Most if not all of the intracellular phenomena of mitosis follow inevitably from very simple assumptions about the physical constitution of the cell and a simple distribution of polarised forces within it, and are likely to prove of only remote and secondary biological significance.

records.text: Early embryological data, up to and well beyond segmentation, are a subject for physiological and physical investigation, and their categories (yolk content, chromosome form and number, radial, bilateral or spiral cleavage) will only seldom and accidentally coincide with the natural or phylogenetic classification of the systematist.

records.text: The cell is a sphere of action of localised forces, of which surface tension gives the cell its outline and individuality; partial versus total segmentation of eggs, and unicellular versus multicellular organisation, differ in whether surface tensions succeed in forming visible separations between cells.

records.text: In naked protoplasmic cells the amoeboid form marks a phase of activity with unequal surface tensions, whereas the spherical form marks a phase of rest when internal homogeneity and minimal potential energy are attained, at which time the cell also becomes encysted.

records.text: The mitochondria, chondriosomes and similar granules and fibrils of cells are not special entities with specific functions but clumps of heterogeneous cell contents gathered by surface tension and drawn out along the cell axis by osmotic currents arising from surface energy and adsorption, revealing a field of force and dynamical polarity in the cell.

records.text: The bulges that begin conjugation in algae such as Pleurocarpus and Mesocarpus, and the root-hair outgrowth of Equisetum spores, arise where surface tension is weakened, and these sites coincide with heavy concentrations of potassium salts, which disperse when the cell becomes symmetrical again.

records.text: In unicellular organisms not only the general configuration but also the departures from symmetry can be correlated with molecular forces, especially local variations of surface tension, acting in their fluid or semifluid surfaces.

records.label: The bee’s cell is a hexagonal prism capped by rhombic-dodecahedral facets

records.text: The regular hexagonal and pyramidal geometry of the bee’s comb is produced automatically by surface tension acting on the cell walls while the wax (or the wasp’s paper pulp) is still semi-fluid, the insects merely building thin tubular cells packed closely together; it is not due to the bee seeking to economise wax.
records.label: Comb geometry arises from surface tension in semi-fluid wax, not bee design

records.text: A perfectly fluid froth of equal cells is divided into Kelvin’s fourteen-sided tetrakaidecahedra, but in plant parenchyma, given restraint and imperfect fluidity, the cells generally take the rhombic dodecahedral form even under symmetrical conditions.
records.label: Parenchyma cells are generally rhombic dodecahedra, ideal froths tetrakaidecahedra

records.text: The whole configuration of an egg in advanced stages of segmentation is determined by simple physical laws just as in the two- and four-celled stages, even though the mathematics becomes too difficult to follow.
records.label: Physical laws govern the whole configuration of later-stage segmenting eggs

records.text: Small changes in the relative sizes of the four cells carry the median partition and its polar furrows through all their possible arrangements, which correspond to those observed in various embryos; these arrangements are physical phenomena distributed without relation to zoological classification, not species characters.
records.label: Polar-furrow arrangements follow relative cell sizes, not species identity

records.text: Although forces other than surface tension act in a growing embryo, there is no evidence at any stage that physical forces cease to govern its material form and are replaced by agencies unknown to physics.
records.label: No evidence that physical forces give way to unknown vital agencies in development

records.text: For a rectangular cell to be divided equally by a partition of least area, the partition must cut across its longest axis, and in successive bisections each new partition must be at right angles to the one before.
records.label: Minimal bisecting walls cut the longest axis and alternate at right angles

records.text: The fundamental rule of cell division is that the incipient partition of a dividing cell takes the least possible area that can divide the given volume; Sachs’s rule of successive divisions at right angles is a subordinate case of this principle.
records.label: A new cell wall has the least area that can enclose the given volume (Errera)

records.text: When a cubical or rectangular cell divides unequally and the smaller part is less than about three-tenths of the whole, the minimal partition is a quarter-cylinder cutting off one corner rather than a plane wall; below about 0.15 of the volume a spherical octant in a corner is smaller still.
records.label: A cell cutting off under ~3/10 of its volume uses a curved corner wall, not a plane

records.text: A flattened cell shaped like a quadrant of a circle divides into equal halves by a circular-arc anticlinal wall meeting the side and periphery at right angles, cutting off about 55° 22′ of the arc and starting about three-tenths of the radius from the centre, since this is the shortest bisecting wall.
records.label: A quadrant-shaped flat cell divides by a curved anticlinal wall about 3:7 along its side

records.text: A sector-shaped (triangular) cell is likely to divide by an anticlinal wall only when its angle of arc lies between about 62½° and 90°; narrower, more tapering cells divide by a periclinal wall, which then has the smaller area.
records.label: Sector cells divide anticlinally only between 62½° and 90°, otherwise periclinally

records.text: Uniform, symmetrical growth of a flattened disc does not imply uniform growth of its cells: after a quadrant divides into triangular and quadrilateral halves, the triangular cell gains area faster and reaches division size first (at about 1.345 times the radius, against about 1.517 for the quadrilateral).
records.label: Uniform growth of a disc makes its daughter cells divide at different times

records.text: Successive minimal-area divisions of a disc soon leave only quadrilateral cells at the periphery, which divide radially, producing a superficial layer of parallel-sided cells (an epidermis) contrasting with the irregular cells beneath.
records.label: Successive minimal-area divisions leave quadrilateral cells forming an epidermis

records.text: A particular arrangement of cell partitions at the eight-celled stage is not a specific or constant character of an organism; within a single species such as the frog, several essentially different arrangements occur.
records.label: The arrangement of the first eight cells is not a constant character of a species

records.text: Because n cells sharing a common outer boundary and meeting three at a time need n − 3 intermediate partitions, every possible grouping of eight cells all reaching the surface belongs to one of thirteen topological types, so all drawings of such eight-celled structures represent one of these types.
records.label: All surface groupings of eight cells belong to one of thirteen types

records.text: Among the possible arrangements of a small group of cells, the most stable (and therefore commonest) are those in which the cell-to-cell contacts are most evenly divided among the cells, and the least stable are those in which one cell has a predominant number of contacts.
records.label: Most stable cell groupings spread contacts evenly; unstable ones concentrate them

records.text: Because a closed surface divided into a small number of faces admits only a small number of arrangements, the same few configurations of cells (and of parts and organs) recur in all kinds of plants and animals with no relation to biological classification.

records.text: The asymmetrical chamber (fossula) of corals such as Heterophyllia and Zaphrentis arises as one of the possible arrangements of septa meeting three at a time, and gives no grounds for interpreting it as a sign of bilaterality or a higher grade of organisation.
records.label: A coral fossula reflects space-partitioning, not higher bilateral organisation

records.text: Because the stomatal mother cell is cut off by a minimal partition whose form depends on epidermal cell shape, stomata are arranged in regular rows where epidermal cells are oblong (as in hyacinth) and irregularly where they are polygonal (as in Sedum).
records.label: Stomata lie in rows on oblong-celled leaves and scattered on polygonal-celled ones

records.text: Pollen grains and spores formed as tetrahedral tetrads keep the plane facets and sharp angles of the tetrad if their walls solidify before the grains separate, but become spherical if they separate while still soft.
records.label: Pollen-grain shape depends on whether walls harden before the tetrad separates

records.text: Because quadrangular cells subdivide by periclinal walls that strengthen the boundary while triangular cells divide by oblique anticlines, outward growth is greater over triangular cells, so buds and outgrowths tend to arise from triangular rather than quadrangular cells, as is widely seen in cryptogams.
records.label: Outgrowths tend to arise from triangular rather than quadrangular cells

records.text: A growing cell divides according to the shape it has reached, set by the ratio of its growth rate to its division frequency: if markedly oblong it divides transversely, if a little more than a hemisphere obliquely, and if less than a hemisphere by a vertical wall along its axis.
records.label: Division plane depends on the ratio of growth rate to division frequency

records.label: Cell division pattern is the result, not the cause, of the form of the growing mass

records.text: Calcareous and other skeletal deposits are, as a rule, precipitated not within actively living protoplasm but in dead or inactive formed material, such as the intercellular matrix or the cell-wall, so their form is not directly shaped by the living cells.
records.label: Skeletal salts precipitate in dead or inactive matrix, not living protoplasm

records.text: Sea-urchin eggs reared in lime-free sea-water develop into apparently healthy larvae that lack the calcareous skeletal rods, and the long larval arms normally supported by those rods are suppressed; the organism can live without the material of its skeleton.
records.label: Sea-urchin larvae reared without lime develop healthily but lack skeletal rods and arms

records.text: The one-handed molecular asymmetry of organic products need not be a prerogative of life; it may have started from a non-vital asymmetric force, such as sunlight circularly polarised by reflection from the sea, which acts unequally on right- and left-handed molecules.
records.label: Biological molecular asymmetry may originate from circularly polarised sunlight

records.text: The concentrically zoned, radiate structure of pearls and of the otoliths of molluscs and bony fishes is essentially the same as that of the calcospherites formed artificially when calcium carbonate is precipitated in albumin, implying the same physico-chemical mode of formation.
records.label: Pearls and bony-fish otoliths share the structure of artificial calcospherites

records.text: Because rhythmic Liesegang precipitation arises from diffusion within the system itself, concentric zones in fish scales, otoliths, bones and starch grains cannot be assumed to record periodic external conditions such as seasons or day and night.
records.label: Concentric growth rings need not record periodic external conditions such as seasons

records.text: Albumin increases the solubility of calcium carbonate and phosphate, whereas its breakdown products dissolve them much less; hence skeletal calcium salts are thrown down when proteins are broken down in metabolism, not by direct action of carbonic acid on a more soluble salt.
records.label: Calcium salts precipitate when the albumins holding them in solution break down

records.text: Skeletal elements comparable in size to a single cell (sponge spicules, radiolarian and foraminiferal skeletons) are shaped by molecular forces such as surface tension, whereas massive skeletons such as vertebrate bones are shaped by gravity, muscle action and mechanical loads, so scale produces essential differences in their controlling forces and forms.
records.label: Cell-sized skeletal elements are shaped by molecular forces, large ones by mechanics

records.text: A spicule tending to grow in a straight line but confined within or against a cell wall grows along a geodetic of the cell surface, so in a spherical or ellipsoidal cell it becomes a circular arc, an elliptic arc or, most often, a portion of a spiral in space, as in C- and S-shaped sponge spicules.
records.label: A straight-growing spicule confined to a cell surface grows along a geodetic

records.text: Holothurian spicules of calcium carbonate reproduce, often indistinguishably, the forms of siliceous sponge spicules, which shows that such spicule forms are determined by the external forces acting during growth (cell confinement), not by the chemical nature or molecular structure of the material.
records.label: Like spicules in silica and calcite show form is set by external forces, not chemistry

records.text: Skeletal material deposited between cells or within their partitions takes the shape of the cell junctions: in a layer of equal cells, where partitions meet in threes at 120°, it forms triradiate spicules with rays at 120°, and in a solid aggregate of four cells it forms tetrahedral four-rayed spicules with rays at about 109°; unequal cells give unequal angles and curved rays.
records.label: Triradiate spicules form at three-cell junctions with rays at 120°, four-rayed at ~109°

records.text: The six-rayed spicules of hexactinellid sponges form because the vesicles that mould them are arranged in linear series (cubic packing) rather than closest packing, so the spicules follow the angles and edges of a system of cubes instead of hexagons or dodecahedra.
records.label: Six-rayed hexactinellid spicules reflect cubic, not closest, packing of vesicles

records.text: Radiolarian species show vague distributions in space and time: many occur worldwide without specific geographic limits, families and genera appear unchanged since the Cambrian, and a small sample of sediment typically contains scores or hundreds of forms with no local predominance of one species.
records.label: Radiolarian species lack definite geographic ranges and many co-occur locally

records.text: The building of agglutinated shells from sand-grains, spicules or diatom frustules by rhizopods such as Difflugia is a purely physical consequence of foreign particles being trapped in the surface film by surface energy, with selectivity explained by specific surface-energies rather than volition.
records.label: Agglutinated protist shells form by surface energy, not choice or skill

records.text: When the outer surface of a radiolarian is covered by a layer of nearly equal froth-like vesicles, silica secreted or adsorbed at the surface collects in the grooves between them, producing a spherical shell of rods in a regular hexagonal network; less regular vesicles give less regular meshes, and repeated layers give concentric shells.
records.label: Hexagonal lattice shells form as silica collects in grooves between surface vesicles

records.text: Spherical hexagonal lattice shells are equally regular whether made of silica (oceanic Radiolaria), strontium sulphate (Acantharia) or an organic chitin-like substance (Clathrulina), showing that their form comes from moulding on an underlying vesicular structure, not from the material.
records.label: Lattice-shell form is independent of the material, being moulded on vesicles

records.text: The skeleton of the nassellarian Callimitra reproduces the interfacial film system of four soap-bubbles in tetrahedral contact (six plane interfaces meeting in threes at 120°, edges meeting near 109°), so it must have been formed at the interfaces of a tetrahedral group of cells.
records.label: Callimitra's skeleton is formed on the interfaces of a tetrahedral group of four cells

records.text: Radiolaria show all five regular polyhedra, including the regular dodecahedron and icosahedron which cannot occur in crystals; therefore the regular radiolarian dodecahedron is not produced by the space-partitioning principles that govern crystallisation.
records.label: Regular dodecahedral radiolarian shells cannot arise by crystal-like space partitioning

records.text: In twenty-spined Radiolaria the spines pass through the facets of a modified hexagonal prism, giving a true hexagonal symmetry of two polar spines, six equatorial spines and two whorls of six intermediate spines; Müller's law of five four-spined circles with no polar spine does not properly apply to any case.
records.label: Twenty-spined Radiolaria have hexagonal symmetry, not Müller's arrangement

records.text: The polar symmetry of the radial spines in Radiolaria cannot be explained by any obvious mechanical forces of the peripheral froth; it arises in the central living protoplasm, and may reflect obscure but still physical directive forces analogous to Lehmann's 'Gestaltungskraft' in fluid crystals.
records.label: Radiolarian axial polarity arises in the central protoplasm, unexplained by mechanics

records.text: The three kinds of geodetic on a cylinder (parallel rings, straight longitudinal lines and helical spirals) are all realised in the local wall thickenings of cylindrical plant cells and vessels, and the helical geodetic in the spiral coils of insect tracheae and tracheids.
records.label: Annular, longitudinal and spiral wall thickenings of plant cells are cylinder geodetics

records.text: On a right cone the spiral geodetic coils more and more closely as the cone narrows, and the sutural line and parallel striations of a turreted spiral shell such as Turritella are geodetics of this kind.
records.label: The suture of a turreted shell is a conical geodetic with coils closing toward the apex

evidence.status: refuted

records.text: In organic structures two opposite systems of geodetic spirals often coexist and interfere, forming a criss-cross arrangement, and this is a very common source of reticulated patterns.
records.label: Two crossing systems of geodetic spirals are a common source of reticulated patterns

records.text: A contractile fibre fixed at both ends on a curved surface first pulls itself into the shortest path on that surface before it can constrict the organ, so the muscle fibres of hollow organs such as the heart, stomach, arteries and intestine automatically lie along geodesics (annular and longitudinal in a simple tube).
records.label: Muscle fibres on hollow organs arrange themselves along geodesic curves

records.text: The heart and stomach develop from simple tubes by dilatation and twisting; their originally circular and longitudinal fibres remain geodetic on the distorted surface, new geodetic systems (such as the oblique stomach fibres) appear on new pouches, and the heart contracts effectively only because its fibres run the shortest course.
records.label: Heart and stomach fibres stay geodetic after the twisting of the primitive tube

records.text: Small ciliated and flagellated organisms cannot steer, but by rotating about their long axis while swimming they convert a constant body-fixed swerve into a continually changing direction in space, so they travel along a helix around a nearly straight axis rather than in a circle.
records.label: Small swimmers rotate about their axis, turning a constant swerve into a helical path

records.text: The permanent spiral forms found in organisms, such as the horns of ruminants, molluscan and foraminiferal shells and the arrangement of florets in the sunflower, are all logarithmic spirals; the outline of a cordate leaf is the one spiral-like organic outline that is not.
records.label: Horns, molluscan shells, foraminifera and sunflower florets follow the logarithmic spiral

records.text: A deflecting force of constant direction acting from outside, such as wind or gravity, can only bend a growing structure towards a limiting direction and never into a spiral; a spiral arises only when the deflecting force is intrinsic to the growing body and turns with the direction of growth, as the columellar muscle does in the snail-shell.
records.label: A spiral needs a deflecting force carried by the growing body, not an external one

records.text: In a tubular structure whose growth is unequal on its two sides, a constant ratio between the rates of growth in the longitudinal and transverse directions generally produces a logarithmic spiral, the value of the ratio fixing the spiral's constant angle, with the circle and the straight line as limiting cases.
records.label: A constant ratio of longitudinal to transverse growth rates yields a logarithmic spiral

records.text: In a scorpioid cyme, where each shoot arises from the last on the same side at an equal angle and successive shoots diminish in length in a constant ratio, the shoots are tangents to a true logarithmic spiral; in the helicoid cyme the same spiral is present but hidden by a superimposed twist.
records.label: The scorpioid cyme traces a true logarithmic spiral

records.text: A spiral shell, like the animal within it, increases in size without changing its shape, even though it grows at one end only; this constant similarity of form under terminal growth is the defining property of the logarithmic spiral and of no other curve.
records.label: The shell grows in size without changing its shape

records.text: In horns, shells and all other organic forms showing a logarithmic spiral, the existing structure is partly old and partly new, and each successive increment of growth is a gnomon to the whole pre-existing structure, that is, an addition that leaves the enlarged whole similar to what it was before.
records.label: Each increment of a spirally grown structure is a gnomon to the whole before it

evidence.status: refuted

records.text: The logarithmic spiral should not be found in structures whose parts are produced simultaneously, such as the margin of a leaf or the contour of a fish, but in hard parts built of successive, permanently retained increments, such as shell, tusk, horn and claw, where it is usually accompanied by lines of growth.
records.label: Logarithmic spirals occur in accreted hard parts, not in simultaneously formed soft parts

records.text: Careful measurement shows that the breadths of successive whorls along a radius of the Nautilus shell, and of spiral ammonitoid and gastropod shells generally, are in geometric progression, so that these shells are logarithmic spirals (for Nautilus each whorl is about three times as broad as the one before).
records.label: Whorl breadths of nautiloid, ammonitoid and gastropod shells form a geometric progression

records.text: The form of any turbinate shell is fixed by a small set of factors (shape of the generating curve, its rate of growth, its rate of rotation about the pole, its rate of translation along the axis, and its inclination), and all differences of form between one shell and another are differences of degree in the relative magnitudes of these factors.
records.label: All differences of form between shells are differences of degree in a few growth ratios

records.text: The constant angle of the logarithmic spiral is about 80° in Nautilus, where each whorl is about three times as broad as its predecessor, and in ordinary ammonitoid and typical spiral gastropod shells is seldom below 80° and usually between 80° and 85°.
records.label: The constant angle of nautiloid, ammonitoid and gastropod spirals is about 80°–85°

records.text: Whether the whorls of a spiral shell stand apart, just touch, or overlap (up to complete involution, as in Nautilus pompilius versus N. umbilicatus) depends only on the ratio of the rate of growth of the outer border of the tube to that of its inner border.
records.label: Separation or overlap of whorls reflects the growth-rate ratio of outer to inner border

records.text: The constant angle of a shell's spiral, like its size, is no evidence of which form is more primitive or ancestral, nor does an intermediate angle show that a shell is intermediate in time or descent; phylogenetic series built from straight, loosely coiled and closely coiled cephalopod shells are not supported by the mathematical study of shell form.
records.label: Spiral constants of shells give no valid evidence of ancestry

records.text: Progressive change of growth ratios along a series of allied forms (orthogenesis) is real in some lineages, and the mathematical study of form can detect such series where they are not obvious, while also showing that strong resemblances of form may arise independently as numerical coincidences.
records.label: Mathematical morphology can reveal orthogenetic series and warn of convergence

records.text: In some ammonoids the spiral angle changes progressively during growth: where it increases the whorls become narrower (as in Oekotraustes), and where it diminishes towards zero the coil opens out into an almost straight curve (as in Scaphites, Ancyloceras and Lituites).
records.label: Ontogenetic change in spiral angle explains narrowing-whorled and uncoiling ammonites

records.text: Shells as different in appearance as Cerithium, Solarium, Natica and Planorbis differ very little in their spiral angle (the ratio of radial to tangential growth) and differ in form mainly in the apical angle of the enveloping cone, which is set by the rate of translation along the axis relative to growth.
records.label: Dissimilar turbinate shells share similar spiral angles and differ mainly in apical angle

records.text: The lines of growth on bivalve shells are not concentric but coaxial curves through the umbo, and they arise because the rate of growth varies as a simple function of direction; in the simplest case the lines are coaxial circles (as in Anomia), and with more complex functions they are coaxial ellipses or other figures (as in Lima or Solen).
records.label: Bivalve growth lines are coaxial curves set by direction-dependent growth rate

records.text: The bivalved carapace of the crustacean Estheria resembles a lamellibranch shell, with lines of growth and a logarithmic spiral of small angle, because its moult is incomplete: each old carapace is retained and the new one grows beneath it and projects beyond its edge.
records.label: Incomplete moulting gives Estheria a mollusc-like spiral shell with growth lines

records.text: The form and direction of brachiopod spiral arms (brachidia) are determined by their initial curvature and the space and pressures within the shell, so that long outwardly directed spirals should go with transversely elongated shells such as Spirifer, inwardly directed spirals with rounded shells such as Atrypa, and discoid spirals with strongly flattened shells.
records.label: Brachiopod spiral arm direction follows shell shape through spatial constraint

records.text: The shell and the aptychus of ammonites are probably the ventral and dorsal portions of a once united conical shell split by unequal growth, as in pteropods; other cephalopods retain only one of the two, the ventral one as the shell of Nautilus and the dorsal one as the shell of Sepia or Spirula.
records.label: Ammonite shell and aptychus are two parts of a once united split cone

records.text: Because a septum is first laid down as an elastic membrane under uniform pressure, it takes the shape of a soap film with the same boundary, a surface of minimal area: spherical in a straight cone with a perpendicular attachment, ellipsoidal with an oblique attachment, and saddle-shaped where the line of attachment is sinuous.
records.label: Cephalopod septa take the form of minimal surfaces like soap films

records.text: The minutely branched, arborescent outline superposed on the lobes and saddles of some ammonite sutures, with branches ending in rounded arcs, is a surface-tension phenomenon of the same kind as the patterns made by milk on a greasy plate or oil on an alkaline solution.
records.label: The fine frilling of ammonite sutures is a surface-tension phenomenon

records.text: Spiral shell forms appear with little relation to the kind of animal producing them, recurring in gastropods, cephalopods, foraminifera and tube worms, and mathematically identical forms recur in every geological period and are found mixed together regardless of climate or local conditions.
records.label: The same spiral shell forms recur across unrelated groups, all ages and all seas

records.text: Natural Selection, in any strictly biological sense, has no necessary share in producing the varied forms of spiral shells, which arise from differences in growth rates and ratios.
records.label: Natural Selection plays no necessary part in producing spiral shell forms

records.text: The form of a single-chambered foraminiferal shell is explained by the laws of surface tension: the protoplasm behaves as a fluid drop whose equilibrium shape is fixed when it acquires its solid covering.
records.label: Single-chambered foraminiferal shells take the form of fluid drops under surface tension

records.text: Foraminiferal shells tend towards a spiral form because they grow by successive increments added to the exterior, each of which becomes a permanent, rigid part of the structure.
records.label: Foraminifera are spiral because they grow by permanent increments added outside

records.label: Septa are convex outwards in Foraminifera and concave in Nautilus because of pressure side

records.text: Spiral foraminiferal shells are logarithmic spirals, recognisable by continued similarity: the large many-chambered shell has the same shape as the smaller, younger shell.
records.label: Spiral foraminiferal shells are logarithmic spirals, large shells similar to small ones

records.text: In Fusulina the breadths of successive whorls stand in the nearly constant ratio 1 : 1.5, which corresponds to a logarithmic spiral with a constant angle of about 86°, like that of ammonites.
records.label: Fusulina whorls increase in ratio 1:1.5, a spiral of constant angle about 86°

records.text: Each foraminiferal chamber bears a constant ratio of size to the next because the rate of increase at each instant is proportional to the whole existing mass of the homogeneous organism.
records.label: Constant chamber-size ratio follows from growth proportional to existing mass

records.text: A mathematical aspect of morphology, largely neglected by morphologists, is interwoven with their problems, complementary to description, and essential to the proper understanding of form.
records.label: A mathematical approach is essential to the study of organic form

records.text: What is most beautiful and regular in natural form, as in the bee's cell, is also found to be most useful and excellent.
records.label: Mathematical regularity and usefulness coincide in living forms

records.text: Living and non-living things alike are governed by the same physical and mathematical laws.
records.label: Living and non-living things are bound alike by physical and mathematical law

records.text: Although theoretical science requires that the systems it studies follow definite rules, those rules need not be the equation-based rules of traditional mathematics; the more general rules embodied in simple computer programs are equally candidates for describing the natural world.
records.label: Rules governing nature need not be those of traditional mathematics

records.text: When simple computer programs are enumerated and run systematically, their behavior is often far from simple, and some of the very simplest programs produce behavior as complex as any known.

records.label: Natural complexity arises because natural systems behave like typical programs

records.text: Describing behavior with mathematical equations succeeds for fairly simple behavior such as planetary motion but almost inevitably fails when behavior is more complex, and descriptions based on natural selection share this limitation; thinking in terms of programs allows meaningful statements about highly complex behavior.
records.label: Equation-based descriptions work for simple behavior but fail for complex behavior

records.text: Across the world of simple programs the same basic forms of behavior occur repeatedly almost independently of the underlying details of the rules, suggesting universal principles of overall behavior that should also apply to systems throughout nature.
records.label: The same basic forms of behavior recur in simple programs regardless of details

records.text: The long-standing difficulty in understanding how thermodynamic behavior, including the Second Law of Thermodynamics, arises in physics can be resolved by a straightforward explanation drawn from the behavior of simple programs.
records.label: Simple programs yield a straightforward explanation of thermodynamic behavior

records.text: Contrary to the assumption that computational universality requires elaborate systems like electronic computers, there exist systems whose rules can be stated in a single sentence that are nevertheless universal, able to perform any possible computation.
records.label: Universal computation is possible in systems with one-sentence rules

records.text: Predicting a system's outcome by a mathematical shortcut is normally possible only for special systems with simple behavior; other systems are computationally irreducible, so their behavior can be found only by tracing each step with roughly as much computational effort as the system itself expends.
records.label: Most systems with non-simple behavior are computationally irreducible

records.text: Computational irreducibility provides an explanation of how humans, even if they follow definite underlying rules, can meaningfully be said to have free will.
records.label: Computational irreducibility explains free will despite deterministic rules

records.text: The complexity found in simple abstract systems leads to fundamental limitations on mathematical proof, of the kind hinted at by Gödel's Theorem, and these limitations are relevant well beyond the narrow scope of current mathematics.
records.label: Complexity of simple abstract systems imposes fundamental limits on proof

records.text: Simple programs can reproduce many features of biological organisms and appear to capture essential mechanisms by which genetic programs generate observed biological forms, enabling new models and general abstract theories in biology.
records.label: Simple programs capture how genetic programs generate biological forms

records.text: Contrary to engineering experience, performing sophisticated tasks does not require correspondingly complicated basic rules; extremely simple underlying rules, potentially implementable directly at the atomic scale, are often sufficient.
records.label: Sophisticated tasks need only extremely simple underlying rules

records.text: Darwinian natural selection does not clearly imply the generation of complexity and in many respects tends to oppose it; a different mechanism, the intrinsic complexity of simple programs, is responsible for most great complexity in biology.
records.label: Natural selection tends to oppose rather than generate complexity

records.text: As a general phenomenon, a system with simple underlying rules started from simple initial conditions can nevertheless show highly complex behavior.
records.label: Simple rules with simple initial conditions can yield highly complex behavior

records.text: The generation of complex behavior from simple rules and simple initial conditions is ultimately responsible for most of the complexity seen in nature.
records.label: Complexity from simple rules accounts for most complexity in nature

records.text: The sequence of cell colors directly below the initial black cell in rule 30 does not repeat in its first million steps, and statistical tests show no meaningful deviation from perfect randomness.
records.label: Rule 30's center column shows no deviation from randomness over a million steps

records.text: Some simple cellular automata, such as rule 110, are more complex than random-looking ones like rule 30: they mix regular regions with interacting localized structures, so that even average properties of their behavior become very difficult to predict.
records.label: Some cellular automata make even average properties hard to predict

records.text: Whether the localized structures in rule 110 eventually annihilate into a regular pattern or proliferate into randomness apparently cannot be determined in advance; the only reliable method is to run the cellular automaton for as many steps as needed.
records.label: Rule 110's fate can be determined only by running it

records.text: Rule 110 started from a single black cell resolves after about 2780 steps: one localized structure survives and interacts with periodic stripes from the left to give behavior that repeats every 240 steps.
records.label: Rule 110 from one black cell becomes periodic with period 240 after about 2780 steps

records.text: Even though every cell of a cellular automaton follows the same rule, different configurations of cell colors can collectively produce many different kinds of behavior, such as regular backgrounds and distinct localized structures.
records.label: Identical cell rules yield diverse behaviors through different configurations

records.text: Because nature is not constrained to predictable designs, systems whose simple rules produce complex behavior, like rule 30 and rule 110, are very common in nature.
records.label: Systems with simple rules and complex behavior are very common in nature

records.label: Complex cellular-automaton-like patterns are absent from historical ornament

records.text: Computers are not limited to computing the consequences of mathematical equations; directly studying the behavior of even the simplest computer programs yields fundamental scientific discoveries.
records.label: Computers enable discoveries beyond working out mathematical equations

records.text: Phenomena not already known to exist can be found only by very systematic and general experiments whose results are examined with as few preconceptions as possible.
records.label: Unknown phenomena are found only by systematic, preconception-free experiments

records.text: A main reason that complexity from simple programs was not discovered before the 1980s is that computer technology powerful enough for the required large-scale exploratory experiments did not yet exist, together with a lack of intuition drawn from practical computing.
records.label: Lack of adequate computers delayed discovery of complexity from simple rules

records.text: Practical computing shows that it is usually very difficult to foresee the behavior of even a simple program, which is why software bugs are so common; the simple structure of cellular automaton rules likewise does not make their behavior easy to predict.
records.label: It is usually very hard to foresee what even a simple program will do

records.text: The prime numbers, though generated by simple rules, have a distribution that seems in many respects random, an early instance of complexity from simple rules that mathematics largely neglected in favor of proving regularities.
records.label: Primes follow simple generating rules yet are distributed seemingly randomly

records.text: Although there were many hints over several centuries, including primes, digits of pi, iterated maps and the Game of Life, the basic phenomenon of simple programs producing complex behavior was never identified before Wolfram's work.
records.label: Complexity from simple programs was never discovered before despite many hints

records.text: Whatever kind of underlying rules a simple program uses (cellular automata, mobile automata, Turing machines, substitution systems, tag systems, register machines, symbolic systems), the overall behavior that emerges falls into the same few basic types first seen in elementary cellular automata.
records.label: Overall behavior types are similar across all kinds of simple programs

records.text: Systems with sufficiently simple rules show only repetition, slightly more complicated rules often add nesting, and complex behavior requires crossing a threshold in rule complexity, but in every kind of system studied this threshold is extremely low.

records.text: Because the typical types of behavior are independent of rule details, one can make fundamental statements about the overall behavior of a natural system without knowing its internal details, and its important features will usually be ones already seen in very simple programs.
records.label: Overall behavior of natural systems can be inferred without knowing their details

records.text: Computer experiments should study the simplest possible systems with the simplest possible procedures, because simple systems already show complex behavior, and the most common mistake is studying systems far more complicated than necessary.

records.text: When systems based on numbers are studied by computer experiment rather than by mathematical analysis, even very simple ones turn out to produce highly complex behavior.

records.text: Simple rules acting only on whole numbers (such as multiplying by 5/2 when even and adding 1 then halving when odd) can produce sequences whose overall sizes fluctuate in a complex, apparently random way with no sign of repetition, so complexity is not just an artifact of looking at digits.

records.text: Even though the primes are generated by a simple sieving rule, the sequence of primes appears in many respects remarkably random.
records.label: The sequence of primes is in many respects random

records.text: Sequences defined by simple properties of numbers (primes, divisor sums, representations as sums of squares or primes) show complexity that persists despite centuries of number theory, and this complexity arises as a fundamental consequence of the rules generating them, just as in other simple programs.
records.label: Complexity in number-theoretic sequences arises from their generating rules

records.text: Despite pi's simple definition, its digit sequence shows no significant regularity in all computed digits and appears for practical purposes completely random.
records.label: The digits of pi are random for practical purposes

records.text: As far as can be determined, the square root of every whole number that is not a perfect square has a digit sequence that appears completely random.
records.label: Square roots of non-square integers have random-looking digits

records.text: Beyond square roots, almost all cube roots, fourth roots, logarithms and exponentials of simple numbers also have apparently random digit sequences.
records.label: Cube roots, logarithms and exponentials also have random-looking digits

records.text: Every rational number p/q has a digit sequence that eventually repeats (with period at most q - 1), and rational numbers are the only numbers with repetitive digit sequences.
records.label: Only rational numbers have repetitive digit sequences

records.text: Nested digit sequences, such as those produced by substitution systems, never correspond to numbers obtainable by taking roots (square roots, cube roots, and so on).
records.label: Roots never have nested digit sequences

records.text: In continued fraction representation, square roots are purely repetitive and e shows definite regularity, but pi, cube roots, fourth roots and similar numbers have continued fraction terms that seem essentially random.
records.label: Continued fractions of pi and higher roots look random

records.text: For any representation of numbers in which recovering the value takes comparable effort for all numbers, some numbers look simple but others produced by simple mathematical operations look random, so such numbers are often intrinsically complex independent of representation.
records.label: Numbers from simple operations are intrinsically complex in any representation

records.text: For a sum of two sine functions Sin[x] + Sin[a x], the arrangement of axis crossings is generated by a generalized substitution system whose rule at each step comes from successive continued fraction terms of (a - 1)/(a + 1), giving nested patterns when a is a quadratic irrational.

records.text: The shift map (doubling modulo 1) generates no randomness of its own: it just moves digits of the initial number leftward, so its output is random only if the initial number's digit sequence was already random.
records.label: The shift map only transcribes randomness from its initial condition

records.text: Some simple iterated maps, such as taking the fractional part of 3x/2, produce behavior that looks random even when started from very simple initial numbers like 1/2, so they intrinsically generate randomness rather than transcribing it from initial conditions.
records.label: Some simple iterated maps generate randomness intrinsically from simple seeds

records.text: Sensitive dependence on initial conditions (the chaos phenomenon) only amplifies differences already present in initial conditions, so on its own it contributes nothing to the ultimate production of randomness, even in systems that also show intrinsic randomness.
records.label: Sensitive dependence on initial conditions does not itself produce randomness

records.text: Cellular automata whose cells take a continuous range of gray levels, updated by simple maps of the neighborhood average, show the same kind of complexity as ordinary discrete cellular automata, and can even show localized structures.
records.label: Continuous cellular automata show the same complexity as discrete ones

records.text: Although almost all traditional models in physics (Maxwell, Einstein, Schrödinger equations) are partial differential equations, nature does not fundamentally follow these continuous mathematical abstractions.
records.label: Nature does not fundamentally follow continuous differential equations

records.text: The dominance of partial differential equations as models in science is in many respects a historical accident of their being solvable by explicit formulas before computers; had computers come earlier, scientific modeling would probably be very different.
records.label: Partial differential equations predominate largely by historical accident

records.text: Complex behavior of the kind seen in simple programs is not restricted to discrete systems: some fairly simple partial differential equations, found by searching, produce highly complex patterns, even with apparently discrete patches.
records.label: Simple partial differential equations can show complex behavior

records.label: Complexity is not rarer in continuous systems, only harder to detect

records.label: Phenomena seen in discrete simple programs also occur in simple continuous systems

records.text: Contrary to what traditional science suggests, going from one to two or more dimensions produces some specific new effects but does not fundamentally change the overall behavior or the occurrence of complexity in simple programs.
records.label: Adding dimensions does not fundamentally change the occurrence of complexity

records.text: The complexity inside patterns generated by two-dimensional totalistic cellular automata is very similar to that of one-dimensional cellular automata: a one-dimensional slice through the 2D pattern evolves much like an ordinary 1D cellular automaton.
records.label: Slices of 2D cellular automata resemble 1D cellular automata

records.text: Some simple two-dimensional cellular automata on a square grid grow patterns whose overall shape closely approximates a perfect circle, despite the grid's square symmetry.
records.label: Simple 2D cellular automata can grow near-perfect circles

records.text: A simple 2D cellular automaton (a cell turns black when exactly three of its eight neighbors are black, otherwise unchanged) can grow patterns whose overall shapes keep changing with no simple form, so complexity can appear in a pattern's overall shape as well as in its interior.
records.label: 2D cellular automata can produce complex overall shapes, not just complex interiors

records.text: Three-dimensional cellular automata show some new specific phenomena but the same basic kinds of behavior as one- and two-dimensional ones, so the phenomenon of complexity does not depend crucially on dimensionality.
records.label: Three-dimensional cellular automata show the same basic kinds of behavior

records.text: Two-dimensional Turing machines behave much like one-dimensional ones: with two or three head states only repetitive and nested behavior normally occurs, and with four states complex behavior is possible but rare (a few rules per million).

records.text: Substitution systems and geometric replacement rules in which each element is replaced independently of other elements, including those of traditional fractal geometry, inevitably produce purely nested patterns.

records.text: Because each sequence in a multiway system always leads to the same successors, the evolution can be represented as a network of which state leads to which, so multiway systems build up their own, often complicated, pattern of connections in time.

records.text: In one dimension, any set of local constraints on cell colors that can be satisfied at all can be satisfied by a simple, purely repetitive arrangement, so simple 1D constraints cannot force complex patterns.
records.label: One-dimensional local constraints can always be met by a repetitive pattern

records.text: Of all 4,294,967,296 two-dimensional constraints defined by allowed templates of a cell and its four neighbors, 766,979,044 cannot be satisfied, and every one of the rest can be satisfied by a repetitive pattern, with 171 repetitive patterns sufficing for all.
records.label: All satisfiable 2D nearest-neighbor template constraints allow repetitive patterns

records.text: Unlike rule-based systems, which can be run directly, systems defined by constraints offer no direct procedure for finding the patterns they allow; one must search from outside the system, which can take enormous computational effort.
records.label: Constraint systems require going outside the system to find their patterns

records.text: Among 2D template constraints that also require one template to appear somewhere, systematic search over more than 18 million constraints finds that the first constraint forcing a non-repetitive pattern (number 18762389) forces a unique nested pattern.
records.label: The simplest constraint forcing a non-repetitive pattern forces a nested one

records.text: Constraints on 3×3 blocks of cells can be constructed to force complex patterns: a set of 56 allowed templates forces a unique, largely random pattern equivalent to the evolution of the rule 30 cellular automaton.

records.text: Unlike simple evolution rules, almost all simple constraints lead only to fairly simple patterns; complex behavior forced by constraints is rare.
records.label: Simple constraints rarely force complex behavior, unlike simple rules

records.text: Because describing complex behavior with constraints requires fairly complicated constraints, the traditional focus of science and mathematics on equations that act like constraints is another reason they failed to identify the phenomenon of complexity.

records.text: Despite differing in detail for almost every rule, the patterns produced by cellular automata of all kinds from random initial conditions can almost always be easily assigned to one of just four classes: uniform final state (class 1), simple stable or periodic structures (class 2), apparently random behavior (class 3), and interacting localized structures (class 4).
records.label: Cellular automaton behavior falls into four basic classes

records.text: Class 4 cellular automata mix order and randomness: they produce localized structures that are individually fairly simple, but which move around and interact with each other in very complicated ways.
records.label: Class 4 consists of simple localized structures interacting in complex ways

records.text: Most detailed properties of cellular automata correlate closely with the four visually defined classes, so that knowing a cellular automaton's class is often enough to predict its detailed properties.
records.label: Detailed cellular automaton properties correlate with the four classes

records.text: For most cellular automata there is no easy way to determine from the underlying rule which class of behavior it will produce; one generally has to run it and see, though some rule forms can be shown to give only class 1 or 2 behavior.
records.label: A cellular automaton's class usually cannot be read off its rule

records.text: Although class 4 is the most complex in appearance, in terms of overall activity it is intermediate between class 2 and class 3, and in sequences of rules it commonly appears at the transition between class 2 and class 3 rules.
records.label: Class 4 lies between class 2 and class 3 in activity

records.text: Cellular automata whose cells take continuous gray-level values show essentially the same four classes of behavior as discrete cellular automata, with class 4 behavior and its discrete localized structures typically appearing at transitions as the rule parameter is varied.
records.label: Continuous cellular automata show the same four classes

records.text: Two-dimensional cellular automata exhibit the same four classes of behavior as one-dimensional ones, which becomes evident when one-dimensional slices through their evolution are examined; class 4 behavior, as in the Game of Life, occurs even on a white background with slightly more complicated rules.
records.label: Two-dimensional cellular automata show the same four classes

records.text: Changing one cell of the initial condition has characteristically different effects by class: in class 1 the change dies out, in class 2 it stays localized, in class 3 it spreads at a uniform rate to affect the whole system, and in class 4 it spreads only sporadically.
records.label: The four classes respond differently to small changes in initial conditions

records.text: Some of the most important features of natural systems can often be understood just by identifying which cellular automaton class their handling of information (forgetting, localized retention, long-range communication) corresponds to.
records.label: Natural systems can be understood by how they handle information

records.text: Class 2 cellular automata are always eventually repetitive because their lack of long-range communication makes each part behave as an independent system of limited size, typically only a few cells across, and hence with short repetition periods.
records.label: Class 2 repetitiveness stems from lack of long-range communication

records.text: A crucial feature of any class 4 cellular automaton is that, although most structures that form eventually die out, there must always be certain structures that can persist forever in it.
records.label: Class 4 systems always have structures that persist forever

records.text: In class 4 cellular automata, whenever sufficiently complicated persistent structures occur, structures that move can eventually be found; moving structures are what allow information to travel and complex class 4 behavior to occur.
records.label: Complicated persistent structures imply moving structures exist

records.text: Class 4 cellular automata can, with appropriate initial conditions, mimic the behavior of all sorts of other systems, including producing unbounded growth of either complex or very simple form.
records.label: Class 4 automata can mimic many other systems

records.text: Although individual persistent structures in class 4 systems such as rule 110 behave fairly repetitively, collisions between them can produce cascades of new structures and outcomes that take very many steps to resolve, yielding behavior of immense complexity from an extremely simple rule.
records.label: Interactions among simple structures in rule 110 give immense complexity

records.text: The same kinds of overall behavior arise regardless of the details of underlying rules, and this universality holds not only among simple programs but also between simple programs and systems in nature, so idealized cell models and real molecular systems should show the same universal features.
records.label: Universal behavior types span simple programs and natural systems

records.text: Apparent randomness in any system arises from one of just three basic mechanisms: continual random input from the environment, randomness transcribed from initial conditions, or intrinsic generation of randomness by the system's own rules with no random input.
records.label: Just three basic mechanisms account for randomness

records.text: The mechanism in which a system's own deterministic rules generate randomness without any random input is ultimately responsible for a large fraction, and perhaps essentially all, of the randomness seen in the natural world.
records.label: Intrinsic randomness generation explains most randomness in nature

records.text: Devices that generate randomness by amplifying microscopic environmental noise (spark gaps, vacuum tubes, semiconductor diodes) have consistently been found to produce output with significant deviations from perfect randomness, because the sampling device relaxes only gradually and because the environment itself has correlations.
records.label: Hardware noise-based random generators deviate from perfect randomness

records.label: Solar system motion should show sensitive dependence over millions of years

records.text: Linear congruential random number generators designed to have maximal repetition period have repeatedly turned out to deviate substantially from perfect randomness (for example, successive outputs plotted as points fall on regular stripes), because the mathematical tractability that guarantees their period also implies regularity.
records.label: Maximal-period linear congruential generators still show strong nonrandomness

records.text: The very possibility of detailed mathematical analysis of a system tends to imply that its output has at least some deviations from perfect randomness, whereas simple rules not constrained by the need for such analysis can generate highly random behavior.
records.label: Amenability to mathematical analysis implies deviations from randomness

records.text: Detailed visual similarities between members of the same species, and between the two symmetric sides of a system, in features that look complex and random cannot be attributed to environmental or initial-condition randomness and must come from intrinsic randomness generation.
records.label: Detailed visual similarities in organisms imply intrinsic randomness

records.text: Systems made of discrete components appear smooth and continuous on large scales mainly because microscopic randomness averages out the discreteness, and it does not matter whether that randomness comes from outside or from intrinsic generation, as shown by random walks, aggregation models and deterministic cellular automata that grow circular shapes.

records.text: Continuous large-scale behavior can arise in a system with discrete components only when there are features that evolve slowly relative to the rate of small-scale random changes; for growth, the random small-scale changes must occur much faster than the overall growth.
records.label: Continuity requires slow features relative to small-scale random changes

records.text: Cellular automata in which a continuous change in initial density of black cells produces a discrete switch in long-time behavior, with whichever color was initially more common taking over the whole system, are fairly rare in one dimension, where domain boundaries often get stuck, but become increasingly common in two and more dimensions.

records.text: Even systems governed by continuous equations, such as certain chemical reaction kinetics, commonly have a limited number of stable states with discrete transitions between them, and because discrete overall behavior is often a system's most obvious feature, discrete models like cellular automata are often the most appropriate.
records.label: Continuous rules can yield discrete behavior, so discrete models often fit

records.text: Almost none of the complex behavior seen in nature is best explained as the satisfaction of constraints, because finding a pattern that satisfies a constraint is usually far too difficult a computation to happen routinely in nature; explicit processes of evolution are the more plausible explanation.
records.label: Complex natural behavior is almost never best explained by constraints
