records.text: For discrete constraint systems the landscape of constraint violations is almost always jagged, so iterative procedures that only move downhill almost invariably get stuck far from a solution, random modifications help only slowly, and no speed-up techniques work well across broad classes of systems; hence natural systems are unlikely to come close to satisfying such constraints.
records.label: Local-improvement procedures get stuck when satisfying discrete constraints

records.text: Unlike identical coins in two dimensions, which readily form the densest hexagonal packing when pushed together, balls in three dimensions pushed together or jiggled almost always get stuck and essentially never reach the densest repetitive packing, which seems obtainable only by careful one-by-one placement.
records.label: Pushed or jiggled spheres do not reach densest packing

records.text: Natural selection can produce forms determined by constraint satisfaction only when those forms are rather simple; complex biological forms are associated instead with explicit evolution rules, mostly those governing the growth of an individual organism.
records.label: Complex biological forms come from growth rules, not selection-driven constraints

records.text: There is no direct correspondence between the complexity of a system's underlying rules and the complexity of its behavior: some of the simplest rules yield highly complex behavior, fairly complicated rules often yield simple behavior, and rules differing at a single position can behave very differently.
records.label: Rule complexity does not determine behavioral complexity

records.text: Nested patterns can arise either from elements splitting or branching into smaller ones or from larger elements being built up from smaller ones (as in additive cellular automata), and the building-up route is probably the more common origin of nesting in nature.
records.label: Nesting in nature mostly arises from building up, not splitting down

records.text: Nesting can arise from random initial conditions through progressive annihilation of randomly placed elements: in essentially any system where domains grow fairly independently and then progressively merge, an overall nested pattern resembling a river-tributary tree forms, even when domain boundaries move as random walks.
records.label: Merging of independently growing domains generically produces nesting

records.text: For systems with complex behavior, a model cannot be adequately assessed by matching a few extracted numbers; the best first test is a visual comparison of the model's overall behavior with that of the real system.
records.label: Models of complex systems should first be judged by comparing overall pictures

records.text: The main features of snowflake shapes are reproduced by a hexagonal cellular automaton in which a cell becomes ice only if exactly one neighbor is ice, which represents the inhibition of nearby growth by released latent heat.
records.label: Snowflake shapes arise from growth inhibition captured by a hexagonal cellular automaton

records.text: During the growth of an individual snowflake its shape should alternate between tree-like and faceted forms, as new branches grow and then collide with one another.
records.label: Growing snowflakes should alternate between tree-like and faceted shapes

records.text: Apparent randomness in the shapes of crystalline materials often arises intrinsically from simple deterministic growth rules, rather than from randomness in the seed or the growth environment.
records.label: Randomness in crystal shapes is often intrinsically generated by simple growth rules

records.text: The roughness and randomness of fracture paths does not come from random irregularities in a material but from a general mechanism in which deterministic interactions of element displacements around a moving crack intrinsically generate randomness, as in a simple cellular automaton model.
records.label: Randomness of fracture surfaces comes from a material-independent intrinsic mechanism

records.text: Any system of particles that conserves quantities such as particle number and momentum and has sufficient microscopic randomness will show the same large-scale fluid behavior, so a discrete cellular automaton particle model can reproduce the flow of real fluids.
records.label: Conservation plus microscopic randomness yields universal fluid behavior

records.text: In almost all cases, large-scale fluid behavior does not depend discernibly on the detailed initial conditions; small perturbations are damped out by viscosity, so sensitive dependence (chaos) is the exception rather than the rule.
records.label: Large-scale fluid flow shows little sensitive dependence on initial conditions

records.text: The randomness seen in turbulent fluids is mostly neither inserted from outside nor inherited from molecular randomness, but is intrinsically generated by the dynamics of the large-scale fluid motion itself.
records.label: Turbulent randomness is intrinsically generated at the level of large-scale fluid motion

records.text: Because turbulent randomness is generated intrinsically by large-scale motion, carefully prepared experiments should produce fluid flows that look random yet are essentially the same on every repeated run.
records.label: Random-looking yet repeatable fluid flows should be producible

records.text: Since iterative random search converges only for simple constraints, the roughly trillion generations of life on Earth are insufficient to find optimal solutions to complex constraints, so most features of organisms are merely good-enough solutions rather than optima.
records.label: Evolution cannot have found optimal solutions to complex fitness constraints

records.text: Most of the complexity seen in biological organisms originates from the abstract fact that many randomly chosen programs produce complex behavior, rather than from adaptation or careful optimization by natural selection.
records.label: Most biological complexity comes from randomly chosen programs, not natural selection

records.text: The complexity of individual parts of organisms, such as textures and other morphological features, was already present in early fossils and has not changed much in at least several hundred million years.
records.label: Complexity of individual organism parts has been roughly constant for eons

records.label: Genetic programs for complex pigment patterns are short

records.text: The power of natural selection is limited: it can systematically optimize only systems or parts of systems whose behavior is simple, and achieves very little when behavior is complex.

records.text: Rather than generating complexity, the main effect of natural selection is to make biological systems avoid complexity, favoring simple, somewhat independent components with smoothly adjustable properties, as in engineered systems.
records.label: Natural selection makes organisms simpler and more engineering-like

records.text: Among related species, the features that differ most rapidly (such as pigmentation and texture patterns) are the ones that show the most obvious complexity, while features under natural selection stay nearly constant.
records.label: Features that change fastest between species are the most complex

records.text: When similar complex structures arise independently in very different organisms, this is because those structures are common outputs of programs of certain kinds, not because they are optimal.
records.label: Convergent structures recur because they are common among programs, not optimal

records.text: Natural selection does not inevitably produce progressively more elaborate organisms; increases in complexity in the fossil record come from random mutations that add features without fatal flaws, while selection's systematic effect is to simplify.
records.label: Natural selection does not inherently drive organisms toward more elaborate structure

records.text: The overall branching patterns of plants, from algae to ferns to trees and flowering plants, are produced by simple growth rules in which each stem tip repeatedly splits into smaller copies of itself at fixed relative lengths and angles.
records.label: Plant branching patterns come from simple substitution-system growth rules

records.text: The shapes of leaves, from smooth to prickly to irregular, are produced by the same simple branching growth process that governs overall plant forms, and small changes in its parameters can change leaf shape greatly.
records.label: Leaf shapes arise from the same simple branching process as whole plants

records.text: The near-universal 137.5° (golden-ratio) angle between successive plant organs is not an optimization found by natural selection but the inevitable result of a simple process where each new element forms where a chemical concentration is highest and depletes it nearby.
records.label: The 137.5° phyllotaxis angle results from a simple inhibition growth process

records.text: Mollusc shell shapes result from secreting material at different rates around the shell opening, and essentially every form produced by a simple growth model with a few parameters is found in some real mollusc.
records.label: Simple growth-rate models generate essentially all mollusc shell shapes

records.text: Because regions of tissue a few tenths of a millimeter across subdivide into regions using different sections of the genetic program (controlled by chemical gradients and homeobox genes), embryos necessarily develop hierarchically, e.g. a leg region before a foot region.

records.text: Pigmentation patterns on mollusc shells are produced line by line by pigment-secreting elements whose new states depend on neighbors' previous states, so the range of shell patterns closely matches the patterns of the simplest symmetric one-dimensional cellular automata.
records.label: Mollusc shell pigment patterns are generated like one-dimensional cellular automata

records.text: The rules generating mollusc shell patterns are effectively chosen at random from the simplest possibilities rather than optimized against predators or for mates, as shown by many species whose patterns are hidden by opaque skin throughout life.
records.label: Mollusc shell pattern rules are effectively random, not optimized

records.text: The few recurring kinds of animal pigmentation patterns (spots, labyrinths, stripes) are produced by a simple rule in which each element tends to match the average color of nearby elements and oppose that of elements further away, as in a two-dimensional cellular automaton.
records.label: Animal coat patterns arise from local activation and longer-range inhibition rules

records.text: Much of the apparent randomness in financial prices, especially on timescales of minutes or seconds, is generated by the internal dynamics of trading entities interacting with one another, not by external news or changes in the value of the asset.
records.label: Short-timescale market randomness comes from internal market dynamics

records.text: In a market modelled as a one-dimensional cellular automaton of buy/sell agents reacting to neighbors, any rule that lets information eventually propagate to all agents makes the running buy-minus-sell total show significant randomness.
records.label: Simple cellular automaton markets generate random-looking price series

records.text: Underneath the known laws of physics there may be a single very simple program from which all known laws, and all the complexity of the universe, emerge.

records.text: Although only a tiny fraction of possible rules are reversible, reversible cellular automata can still produce behavior, including apparent randomness and localized structures, as complex as that of non-reversible systems.

records.text: If the ultimate rule for the universe is simple, it cannot realistically be found by engineering it from observed features; the only practical method is to choose a straightforward representation and systematically search through large numbers of candidate rules.
records.label: The fundamental rule cannot be found by working backwards from known laws

records.text: Features such as seemingly continuous space and certain aspects of gravitation and quantum mechanics will emerge from many different underlying rules for the universe, whereas properties like the spectrum of particle masses, and perhaps the dimensionality of space, will be specific to particular rules.
records.label: Space, gravity and quantum features are generic across many candidate rules

records.text: Most physical laws discovered so far are not fundamental but are emergent large-scale features of an underlying rule, so their simplicity says little about the simplicity of that rule.
records.label: Most known physical laws are emergent, not fundamental

records.text: Space, though experimentally continuous down to about 10^-20 meters, is very likely made of discrete elements at still smaller scales, just as fluids and other seemingly continuous things have turned out to be.
records.label: Space is discrete below the scales probed by experiment

records.text: In the simplest ultimate model of the universe there is no distinction between space and its contents: matter and everything else are made of the same underlying structure as space, unlike in a cellular automaton.
records.label: Space and matter should be made of the same stuff

records.text: At the lowest level, space is most likely a giant network of nodes defined only by their connections (and it suffices to consider nodes with exactly three connections), with ordinary space emerging as a large-scale limit.
records.label: At the lowest level space is a network of nodes

records.text: A network corresponds to ordinary d-dimensional space exactly when the number of nodes within graph distance r of a node grows in a limiting sense like r^d; tree-like or randomly connected networks correspond to no finite dimension.
records.label: Network dimension is set by growth of node counts with distance

records.text: An observer embedded in a system such as a mobile automaton cannot see its individual update steps; all the observer can perceive is the network of causal relationships between updating events, so perceived time and spacetime derive purely from that causal network, and sequential updating can appear as synchronized parallel evolution.
records.label: Observers perceive time only through the causal network of events

records.text: A substitution system whose rules replace only blocks that can never overlap themselves or each other always yields the same causal network regardless of the order in which replacements are applied (the property Wolfram calls causal invariance).
records.label: Non-overlapping replacement rules give update-order-independent causal networks

records.text: Although the universe has no global clock and its rules may be applicable in arbitrary order, its actual rules most likely have the property of always yielding the same causal network, and so a unique perceived history.
records.label: The universe's rules likely yield a unique causal network

records.text: The ultimate rules for the universe will produce networks that look largely random at small scales, and this randomness is what allows a definite and robust dimensionality of 3 to emerge for space.
records.label: Small-scale randomness in the network makes space robustly 3D

records.text: If the underlying rules of the universe are causal invariant, then slices through the causal network at different angles, corresponding to different uniform velocities, are all governed by the same rules, so physics is the same regardless of uniform motion and the standard phenomena of special relativity such as time dilation follow.
records.label: Causal invariance yields special relativity

records.text: Although observed elementary particle masses are not in simple ratios (unlike electric charges), truly fundamental particle masses may still have simple relations, because observed masses include varying amounts of interaction energy.

records.text: The basic mechanisms underlying human perception and scientific analysis, like the mechanisms behind many natural processes, can be captured by simple programs based on simple rules.
records.label: Perception and analysis are themselves carried out by simple programs

records.text: Although inferring the generating procedure from observed behavior is fairly easy for the rules of traditional mathematics, for general simple programs it is often extremely difficult, because their complex output shows no obvious trace of its simple origin.
records.label: Recovering a simple rule from its complex output is usually very hard

records.text: Defining something as random only when no short description of it exists at all is too restrictive and uncomputable (it would mean deterministic rules can never generate randomness), so any useful definition of randomness must refer to how short descriptions are to be found.
records.label: Randomness cannot usefully be defined only by the existence of short descriptions

records.text: Since essentially all standard methods of perception and analysis are based on simple programs, something should be considered random whenever essentially no simple program succeeds in detecting regularities in it.
records.label: Something is random if essentially no simple program detects regularities in it

records.text: Once a few simple programs corresponding to standard methods of perception and analysis have failed to detect regularities in some data, it is extremely rare for any other simple program to succeed, so the everyday judgment of randomness is in practice fairly unambiguous.
records.label: If a few standard tests find no regularity, other simple programs rarely do

records.text: To call something complex is to say that our methods of perception and analysis have failed to find a short description of the features of it that we are interested in; complexity therefore depends on which features one chooses to capture.
records.label: Complexity means our perception and analysis fail to find a short description

records.text: People tend to lose interest in images with no simple features (such as perfectly random ones), and the images that hold attention and seem most aesthetically pleasing are those in which some features are simple to describe while others have no short description findable by human visual perception.
records.label: Most engaging images mix simply describable and indescribable features

records.text: Structurally different lossless data compression methods (run-length, block/Huffman, pointer-based and two-dimensional schemes) have remarkably similar capabilities: they compress uniform regions, repetitive behavior and to some extent nested behavior, but achieve no substantial compression of more complex behavior even when it is generated by very short programs.
records.label: Data compression methods all compress repetition and nesting but little else

records.text: Under lossy compression by keeping only some basic forms (as in JPEG-like schemes), the relevant features of both simple and completely random images remain recognizable at high compression, whereas images normally considered complex need much lower compression, and reordering the basic forms does not change this substantially.
records.label: Complex images lose recognizable features under lossy compression

records.text: Human perception generally works by cells responding to specific fixed features and ignoring others; in vision, cortical cells act as templates for small local patterns, and textures are distinguished by the densities of such local features, much as colors are distinguished by densities of red, green and blue.
records.label: Texture is perceived through densities of simple local features

records.text: Humans can readily see by eye that a two-dimensional pattern is purely repetitive, but generally cannot tell that a pattern is nested (unless it is dominated by large uniform areas), even though a simple two-dimensional pointer-based encoding recognizes the nesting.
records.label: Human vision easily detects repetition but generally fails to detect nesting

records.text: For sounds generated from sequences with fairly uniform properties, the human auditory system recognizes only exact or approximate repetition at definite frequencies; nested or other non-repetitive structure, beyond a few large spectral peaks, is heard as random noise.
records.label: Hearing detects repetition at definite frequencies and essentially nothing else

records.text: When probabilistic models such as block-frequency, Markov or probabilistic cellular automaton models are fitted to data generated by deterministic cellular automata, they reproduce the statistics used in fitting but their typical behavior is considerably more random and misses most detailed features of the data.
records.label: Best-fit probabilistic models of deterministic data look more random than the data

records.text: Checking that all blocks of all lengths occur with equal frequency does not guarantee absence of regularity: sequences such as linear feedback shift register output or concatenated binary digits of successive integers have accurate block frequencies yet are non-random, as revealed for instance by an abnormally small spread of those frequencies.
records.label: Equal block frequencies of all lengths is not a universal randomness test

records.text: Retrieval from memory on the basis of similarity underlies almost every major aspect of human thinking, including generalization, analogy and intuition, and logical reasoning is not fundamental but is itself carried out by retrieving learned patterns of argument from memory.
records.label: Memory retrieval, not logic, underlies almost all of human thinking

records.text: Despite the complicated construction of the brain, there is a core to human thinking that is largely independent of neural details and is based on rather simple rules, with nothing fundamentally special about the processes involved.
records.label: The core of human thinking is based on rather simple rules

records.text: Because complex behavior from simple rules is hard to direct to specific tasks, it will likely be much easier to reproduce general human-like thinking than a special version of human-like thinking restricted to specific tasks; a recognizably human-like system would also need a human-like base of experience.

records.text: The most important idea underlying Wolfram's new kind of science is computation: systems such as cellular automata should be viewed as computations, with initial conditions as input and later states as output, so that systems with entirely different rules can be discussed in a unified, abstract way.
records.label: Computation is the central organizing idea of the new science

records.text: Any system whatsoever, not just a cellular automaton, can be viewed as performing a computation that determines what its future behavior will be.

records.text: Although universality has never before been seriously considered in natural science, it is crucial for finding general ways to characterize and understand the complexity seen in natural systems.
records.label: Universality is crucial for understanding complexity in natural systems

records.text: Because a universal system can emulate any other system, it can produce behavior as complex as that of any other system, so knowing a system is universal implies it can produce behavior that is in a sense arbitrarily complex.
records.label: A universal system can produce arbitrarily complex behavior

records.text: Contrary to the assumption that universality is rare and found only in systems specifically constructed to have it, universality is a widespread phenomenon that also occurs in a wide range of important systems found in nature.
records.label: Universality is widespread and occurs in many systems in nature

records.text: A single cellular automaton with fixed rules (Wolfram's 19-color, next-nearest-neighbor construction) can, given suitable initial conditions, emulate any cellular automaton whatsoever, regardless of how many colors or neighbors its rules involve, including rules more complicated than its own.
records.label: A fixed universal cellular automaton can emulate any cellular automaton

records.text: Cellular automata can be set up to emulate almost every type of system considered in the book—mobile automata, Turing machines, substitution systems, sequential substitution and tag systems, register machines, arithmetic systems, logic circuits and random-access memory—and in principle a practical computer in its entirety.
records.label: Cellular automata can emulate nearly all other system types, even computers

records.text: Unlike mobile automata or Turing machines, substitution systems cannot in general be emulated one step per cellular automaton step, because the number of elements in a substitution system can be multiplied by a factor each step while a cellular automaton pattern can grow only by a fixed amount per step; progressively more cellular automaton steps are needed per substitution step.
records.label: Cellular automata cannot emulate substitution systems step for step

records.text: Neighbor-independent substitution systems can only generate repetitive or nested patterns, so they cannot emulate cellular automata such as rule 30, whereas neighbor-dependent substitution systems can emulate cellular automata straightforwardly.
records.label: Neighbor-independent substitution systems cannot emulate cellular automata

records.text: Since a universal cellular automaton exists, any type of system shown capable of emulating any cellular automaton—including mobile automata, Turing machines, neighbor-dependent and sequential substitution systems, tag systems, cyclic tag systems, symbolic systems and register machines—must contain universal examples.
records.label: Any system type that can emulate every cellular automaton has universal members

records.text: A system that repeatedly takes a whole number, computes its remainder modulo a constant and applies an arithmetic operation chosen by that remainder can emulate a register machine, and is therefore universal; given how widespread universality is, arithmetic supporting it is unsurprising.
records.label: Simple arithmetic systems based on remainders can be universal

records.text: Because essentially all the kinds of systems studied (cellular automata, Turing machines, substitution systems, register machines and others) can emulate each other, a wide variety of systems with very different underlying structures are fundamentally equivalent in the computations they can perform, so computation can be studied abstractly with results applying across systems.
records.label: Structurally different systems are computationally equivalent

records.text: The universality of rule 110, one of the simplest possible cellular automaton rules, implies that universality is far more common than previously thought and should occur in a very wide range of systems, including many with rather simple rules.
records.label: Universality should be common, including among very simple rules

records.text: As rules become progressively more complicated, overall behavior grows more complex only until the threshold of universality is reached, and since that threshold is very low, behavior beyond the very simplest rules of any kind should quickly become as complex as it will ever be—consistent with the Chapter 3 survey.

records.text: Cellular automata that produce only uniform or repetitive patterns (class 1 and class 2) can never be universal, because they transmit information only over limited distances and so support only processes involving a limited number of cells.

records.text: Cellular automata whose information transmission is highly constrained so that patterns are essentially nested, and additive rules such as rules 90 and 150 whose states after a power-of-two number of steps are simple superpositions of shifted copies of the initial condition, cannot be universal.
records.label: Nested-pattern and additive cellular automata cannot be universal

records.text: Rule 54, a possible class 4 elementary cellular automaton, shows only repetitive or nested behavior in its first hundred million initial conditions, leaving it uncertain whether rule 54 is universal.
records.label: Rule 54 shows only repetitive or nested forms in 100 million initial conditions

records.text: More or less any system whose behavior is not fundamentally repetitive or nested will in the end turn out to be universal, so there is a close connection between universality and the appearance of complex behavior, though proving it will be far easier for some systems (such as rule 110) than others.
records.label: Any non-repetitive, non-nested system is expected to be universal

records.text: Universality proofs proceed by building components from localized structures, which requires controlled transmission of information; in class 3 systems a change to a single cell eventually spreads to all cells, making it very hard to identify definite components and hence to prove universality.
records.label: Uncontrolled information flow in class 3 rules hinders universality proofs

records.text: Although the localized structures found in rules 30 and 45 on repetitive backgrounds all move at the same speed and so cannot interact, preventing a rule 110-style proof, rules 30 and 45 will nevertheless turn out to be universal.
records.label: Rules 30 and 45 are expected to be universal

records.text: Using block encodings, elementary rules with complex behavior such as rules 22, 30 and 110 can be made to emulate a single step of all 256 elementary cellular automata, whereas rules with simple behavior such as 90 and 184 can emulate only a few; this supports the idea that complex-looking cellular automata can do arbitrarily sophisticated computations.
records.label: Complex elementary rules can emulate one step of every elementary rule

records.text: Since elementary cellular automata whose behavior looks complex can do computations as sophisticated as desired, they are expected to be universal, so perhaps as many as 27 of the 256 elementary rules are universal.
records.label: Perhaps as many as 27 of the 256 elementary rules are universal

records.text: A Turing machine with just 2 states and 5 colors, far simpler than the 7-state 4-color machine that had long been the simplest known, is universal because it emulates rule 110 by sweeping back and forth and updating all cells by one rule 110 step per sweep.

records.text: Starting from a blank tape, roughly one in 50,000 2-state 4-color Turing machines and one in 200,000 4-state 2-color machines show complex behavior, and 14 essentially equivalent machines among the 2,985,984 with 2 states and 3 colors do so.

records.text: The 2-state 3-color Turing machine numbered 596,440, which yields complicated behavior from a blank tape, is likely universal, and if so would by most measures be the simplest universal Turing machine.

records.text: Combinators, symbolic systems long known to be universal, show highly complex behavior despite simple rules—for example a length-8 initial expression grows exponentially with seemingly random internal structure—and they can emulate rule 110, suggesting their universality is just associated with general complex behavior.
records.label: Combinators show highly complex behavior despite simple rules

records.text: Any process that follows definite rules, including processes in nature governed by physical law as well as processes constructed by humans, can be viewed as a computation, giving a uniform framework for comparing very different processes.
records.label: Every process, natural or artificial, can be viewed as a computation

records.text: Almost all processes whose behavior is not obviously simple correspond to computations of equivalent sophistication; there is essentially a single highest level of computational sophistication, and almost all such processes reach it regardless of how simple their rules or initial conditions are.
records.label: Principle of Computational Equivalence: one maximal level of sophistication

records.text: As a law of nature, no system that can actually be constructed in our universe can carry out explicit computations more sophisticated than those of universal systems such as cellular automata and Turing machines; imaginable hypercomputers (e.g. with infinite tables of results) cannot be built.
records.label: No physical system can compute beyond cellular automata and Turing machines

records.text: Among all possible rules of a given type (such as cellular automata) whose behavior is not obviously simple, i.e. not repetitive or nested, the overwhelming majority are computationally universal, so universality is extremely common rather than a rare engineered property.
records.label: An overwhelming fraction of non-simple rules are universal

records.text: When no constraint such as engineering design or natural selection forces simple behavior, the rules that operate in nature are effectively selected in no special way apart from tending to be structurally simple, so they behave like randomly chosen rules and are almost always universal when their behavior is not obviously simple.
records.label: Rules occurring in nature are typically not specially selected

records.text: The pattern generated by the rule 30 cellular automaton from a single black cell appears to contain every possible block of cells eventually, so that essentially any possible computation exists somewhere within this single pattern.
records.label: Rule 30 from a single cell contains every possible block

records.text: Although simple molecules may settle into minimum-energy configurations, complicated molecules typically do not; they explore configurations by an explicit evolution process, so nature does not actually solve hard constraint-satisfaction problems as traditional models idealize.
records.label: Complicated molecules generally do not reach minimum-energy configurations

records.text: For computationally irreducible systems, even with complete knowledge of rules and initial conditions, there is no way to predict the behavior except by performing almost as many computational steps as the system's own evolution.
records.label: Computational irreducibility blocks shortcuts to predicting behavior

records.text: Behavior that is obviously simple, such as repetitive or nested behavior, is always computationally reducible, while in practically all other cases behavior is computationally irreducible.
records.label: Only obviously simple behavior is reducible; nearly all else is irreducible

records.text: Traditional theoretical science, including its use of mathematical formulas, relies on computational reducibility, which is the fundamental reason it has made little progress with systems whose behavior is not quite simple and why it has tended to restrict its domain to reducible phenomena.

records.text: Computer simulation is not merely a convenient substitute for mathematical formulas: there are many common systems whose behavior can be determined only by something like explicit simulation, and there can be no easy theory for almost any behavior that seems complex.

records.text: For cellular automata with nested behavior such as elementary rules 60 and 188, the color of a cell after t steps can be found in about log2(t) steps from the base-2 digits of its position, rather than by tracing all t steps.

records.text: Systems whose behavior looks complex but is nevertheless computationally reducible, such as the cellular automaton that generates digits of powers of 2, are very rare; in the vast majority of cases complex-looking behavior in nature and elsewhere is computationally irreducible.

records.text: The apparent freedom of human will arises because, although brain components follow definite laws, the brain's overall behavior is an irreducible computation whose outcome cannot be found by reasonable laws; no external influence, chaos, or quantum randomness is needed.
